Article Title: Apple layoffs hit employees across teams; company confirms job cuts, says: While we will create new roles as part of this change, it will also...
Article Text:
Apple has laid off more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro

Apple Vision Pro layoffs: gaming team shut down, immersive video crew cut back

Siri job cuts explained: new AI architecture needs a different kind of engineer

Apple smart glasses take priority as Vision Pro waits for 2028

Apple has laid off more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro, according to a Bloomberg report by Mark Gurman. The split is roughly even. About 100 roles have gone from the Vision Pro organisation, and about 100 more from Siri and the software groups around it. Also caught in the round is Intelligent Systems Experience, a team inside Apple's software engineering arm that builds AI features sitting across iPhone, iPad and Mac.Apple confirmed the cuts without confirming the number. The company said it is realigning teams "to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users," and that new roles are being created even as existing ones disappear. Staff who lost jobs can apply elsewhere inside Apple. What makes this round worth reading closely is that one headcount figure is hiding two completely different stories. One team is being rebuilt. The other is being told to wait.The headset took the harder blow. Apple has largely closed the group working on Vision Pro gaming and shrunk the team producing immersive video, the 3D content Apple has used as the device's showpiece since launch. That content is expensive in a way the sales figures could not support.A single episode can run into several million dollars, shot by multiple crews of Apple staff and contractors, for an audience that stayed small. AppleInsider reported the first wave a day before Bloomberg, putting at least 60 layoffs across Apple's VR teams. Films like Submerged will still get made, just fewer of them, with outside studios expected to pick up the slack. Gaming never arrived at all. The most capable VR workaround on the platform, iVRY, still needs a Windows PC plugged in to work.Siri's situation is the opposite of a wind-down. The assistant is being rebuilt on a new technical architecture for its AI version, and that stack asks for skills the old one did not. So some roles end, resources move, and new positions open around the rebuilt assistant. Apple showed the revamped Siri at WWDC this year and a public beta is due before 2026 closes. Nobody cuts a team weeks before shipping unless the team they need looks different from the one they have.Vision Pro arrived in February 2024 at $3,499 and now sells for $3,699, close to Rs 3.2 lakh, after component costs forced a rise. Heavy, costly, thin on reasons to wear it daily. Apple insists visionOS is not going anywhere, and visionOS 27 shipped in June to prove it. A new headset is still penciled in for as late as end-2028. Meanwhile Bloomberg reports work with Samsung Display on an entry-level XR display was suspended, and Apple is aiming to announce smart glasses at WWDC 2027 and ship them that year. Those glasses will not run immersive video or heavy games.Incoming CEO John Ternus now owns the decision. Apple has not given up on a screen you wear on your face. It has given up on this one being the version people buy.
Article Summary: Apple has laid off more than 200 people across the teams building Siri and the Vision Pro, according to a Bloomberg report. Apple confirmed the cuts without confirming the number. The split is roughly even. About 100 roles have gone from Vision Pro organisation, and about 100 more from Siri and software groups around it.

Article Title: How an accidental discovery by underconstruction Telescope in Chile captured one of Astronomy’s missing links
Article Text:
The Helix nebula, imaged here, lies 650 light-years away in the constellation Aquarius. (Image credit: Nasa)

Successful test run in the Atacama

How the Telescope uncovered the faint bow shocks

Low-cost engineering behind MOTHRA

An unfinished, custom-built observatory in Chile has unexpectedly solved one of puzzles astrophysics struggled with by directly capturing dense clouds of gas expelled by a dying star blending back into the Milky Way galaxy. As detailed in a study published in the journal Nature, the breakthrough demonstrates the exact physical mechanism through which foundational elements like carbon and oxygen, which are created deep within stellar cores, are recycled to serve as the building blocks for future stellar nurseries, planetary bodies and living organisms.The milestone occurred by chance during calibration tests in November 2025. Scientists were in the middle of assembling a composite optical instrument designed to link hundreds of commercial, off-the-shelf telephoto camera lenses into a unified composite array.With less than 200 of its targeted 1,140 lenses mounted, researchers aligned the array toward the Helix Nebula, which is an expansive, radiant ring of gas located approximately 650 light-years away from Earth. The nebula represents the remnants of a Sun-like star that cast off its external shell in its death throes.While researchers have long theorised that expelled stellar envelopes enrich the surrounding interstellar medium to seed future celestial bodies, documenting this dispersal in real time had eluded previous observational attempts.Despite running at a fraction of its final hardware capacity, the observatory detected 22 dimly illuminated arcs extending into the outer halo well beyond the Helix Nebula's primary bright ring. Researchers interpret glowing arcs as bow shocks, which resemble the wake pushed in front of a moving vessel. These are formed as dense pockets of ejected matter crash through the surrounding interstellar medium.Bow shocks situated further from the core appear distinctly smaller, softer and more fragmented, illustrating how the traveling clouds break down and dissolve into surrounding space over an estimated span of roughly 10,000 years.Commenting on the images, University of British Columbia astronomer Sun Kwok, who was not part of the research team, highlighted that the findings deliver critical new insights into how stellar mass loss interacts with interstellar space.The breakthrough imagery was recorded by the Modular Optical Telephoto Hyperspectral Robotic Array (MOTHRA), situated at Chile’s El Sauce Observatory. Constructed for a few tens of millions of dollars with financial backing from XTX Markets founder and CEO Alex Gerko, MOTHRA is scheduled for full operational completion by the end of this year.Modeled after its predecessor, the Dragonfly array in New Mexico, MOTHRA’s primary objective is tracing the faint filaments of the cosmic web that connect distant galaxies, where vast reserves of matter produce extremely faint light signals.
Article Summary: Unfinished, custom-built observatory in Chile captured dense clouds of gas expelled by a dying star blending back into the Milky Way galaxy. The breakthrough demonstrates the exact physical mechanism through which foundational elements like carbon and oxygen are recycled. The milestone occurred by chance during calibration tests in November 2025.

Article Title: Intel study reveals surge in enterprise robotics adoption but 3 gaps threaten deployment
Article Text:
Intel highlights disconnect between fleet ambition and planning

Enterprise robotics adoption is expanding, yet critical deficits across operational strategy, talent, safety frameworks and edge infrastructure risk limiting organisations from scaling successfully, according to new research commissioned by Intel. The study, titled The Robotics Readiness Gap, surveyed 800 executive decision-makers, IT managers, robotics engineers, and public sector officials across the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, China and South Korea, representing enterprises generating over $500 million in annual revenue.The findings confirm that autonomous systems are no longer treated as experimental trials, with organisations already recording tangible gains across operational speed, quality control, and workplace output.The report identifies a divide between enterprise deployment targets and organisational preparedness.The report says that 60% of senior executives anticipate running active fleets of robots within the next five years, with many projecting that full integration could double total operational productivity. While 74% of respondents believe workforce planning and robotics roadmaps will be fully unified by 2030, and 67% express confidence in supervising integrated human-robot teams by that date, only 40% currently maintain a documented, formal human-robot workforce framework.John Healy, vice president and general manager of Intel’s Industrial and Robotics Division, noted that the upcoming phase of robotics deployment will not hinge on basic technical capability, but on whether enterprises are prepared to scale. He noted that businesses embedding robotics and Physical AI directly into their primary workflows – not as add-ons – will capture the true economic return.The research outlines five essential pillars that determine whether an organisation successfully scales automation or remains trapped in pilot phases. Despite two-thirds of executives expecting to manage collaborative human-robot teams by 2030, just four in ten have established the structural blueprints necessary to govern them.About 67% of leaders expect automation to upskill human employees—not devalue them. However, 40% say severe talent and skills shortages are currently hindering scaling efforts. Automation’s biggest dividend is workplace safety, according to 31% of respondents, but 55% of them acknowledge that safety concerns have delayed projects. Sixty-eight percent say common international safety standards would speed up implementation.Nearly 77% prefer functional reliability over visual design but 65% believe that modern physical robot designs are constrained by hardware limitations rather than operational needs More than three-quarters of leaders say mission-critical tasks require response times of less than 100 milliseconds, with almost a quarter needing to be executed in less than 10 milliseconds. Currently, 42% have defined funding for edge and on-device AI architectures, and 39% are developing their strategy.
Article Summary: Intel report highlights disconnect between fleet ambition and planning for robots. 60% of senior executives anticipate running active fleets of robots within the next five years. Only 40% currently maintain a documented, formal human-robot workforce framework. Only 42% have defined funding for edge and on- device AI architectures.

Article Title: FTC urged to investigate AI companies over ‘buying and destroying books to train models’
Article Text:
As artificial intelligence companies seek vast quantities of human-written content, concerns are mounting over reports that some rare books are being dismantled and digitised for AI training.

What the letter says

A coalition of over a dozen advocacy and civil society groups has reportedly urged the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to launch a formal inquiry into major artificial intelligence (AI) companies for allegedly purchasing, scanning and physically destroying print books to train their machine learning systems. In a joint petition initially obtained by Axios, organisations including the Consumer Federation of America, Demand Progress Education Fund and the Institute for Local Self-Reliance asked federal regulators to inspect what they describe as a destructive and aggressive data collection method employed by entrenched AI market leaders.The report says that if the FTC acts on the request, the regulatory debate surrounding training data could transition from intellectual property disputes into an antitrust and market competition battle under which, federal regulators would evaluate whether major tech companies are intentionally eliminating physical source material to deny upstart competitors the resources needed to build rival systems.Citing court records, The Washington Post reported in January that AI developer Anthropic expended millions of dollars purchasing books, stripping their spines to digitize the pages, and feeding the text into its Claude model. The publication noted that Google, OpenAI and Microsoft have faced comparable copyright challenges.The letter warns that this tactic threatens to permanently erase rare and out-of-print volumes from the public domain, as technology corporations acquire and scrap the final remaining print editions.The petition argues that purchasing and destroying print media represents an unfair method of competition designed to starve the wider market of essential training inputs.“We urge the FTC to view this practice not in isolation but rather as the latest escalation in a documented pattern of anticompetitive conduct designed to create an insurmountable systemic moat around AI incumbents,” the groups wrote.The coalition explained that unlike conventional data collection, this “hoard-and-destroy” approach functions as an artificial economic barrier, increasing operating costs for smaller entrants and cutting off emerging startups from the underlying content required to compete.
Article Summary: A coalition of over a dozen advocacy and civil society groups has reportedly urged the US Federal Trade Commission to launch a formal inquiry into major artificial intelligence (AI) companies. The petition argues that purchasing and destroying print media represents an unfair method of competition designed to starve the wider market of essential training inputs.

Article Title: How AI memory boom is creating hundreds of millionaires in 1350 kilometres away from Silicon Valley in Idaho
Article Text:
PC: Nasa

Local expansion and economic impact

Located roughly 1,350 kilometres away from Silicon Valley, the Mountain West city of Boise is experiencing a surge in wealth creation, areport has said. Fueled by increasing global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) hardware, local memory chipmaker Micron has seen its market value cross $1 trillion, minting hundreds of new millionaires among long-term employees and area residents. According to a report by CNBC, local financial advisor Dave Petso, who has managed assets in Boise for 45 years through the dot-com crash and the 2008 recession, previously considered the hometown semiconductor manufacturer an unexciting corporate operation and a poor investment.Following a more than ten-fold stock surge since late 2024, Petso spends much of his time helping local clients diversify portfolios that previously held $20,000 in equity and are now worth hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars.The influx of capital is reshaping Boise, a community of 250,000 traditionally known for outdoor recreation and Boise State University's blue turf football field. Micron has started construction on two local fabrication facilities projected to generate over 17,000 regional jobs, including 3,500 direct roles at Micron, which already employs roughly 7,000 workers locally.The company has also announced the establishment of Micron Research Labs in Boise, backed by a $10 billion investment over the next ten years, with construction starting next year.Meanwhile, Meta is constructing an $800 million data facility in nearby Kuna, Idaho, while key suppliers such as Lam Research and cleanroom contractor Exyte are opening regional offices.Rapid industrial expansion has created growing pains for long-term residents. Locals complain of severe traffic congestion, rising property prices and an influx of newcomers who are reportedly altering local culture.Citing data from leading real estate marketplace Zillow, the report says that average rents in Boise increased 4.3% over the past year while the nationwide rates declined. Resident and tech entrepreneur Jason Crawforth noted that while stock gains have increased his net worth, the rising costs are eroding the low cost of living that once served as the city’s primary competitive advantage.
Article Summary: Micron has seen its market value cross $1 trillion, minting hundreds of new millionaires among long-term employees and area residents. Micron has started construction on two local fabrication facilities projected to generate over 17,000 regional jobs. Locals complain of severe traffic congestion, rising property prices and an influx of newcomers who are altering local culture.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jack Dorsey: “Everyone has an idea. But it’s really about executing the idea and…” - simple lesson about taking the first step
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jack Dorsey

“Everyone has an idea. But it’s really about executing the idea and attracting other people to help you work on the idea.”

What Jack Dorsey meant by the quote

Why having an idea is only the beginning

The role of other people in turning ideas into reality

Jack Dorsey’s early interest in technology

How Dorsey turned a simple payment idea into Square

Execution means testing an idea against reality

Why collaboration can change the original idea

The difference between an idea and a working product

What Dorsey’s quote means for everyday projects

Why the quote remains relevant

Lessons learnt from Jack Dorsey’s quote

An idea needs action to become useful.

You do not have to build everything alone.

Execution reveals what an idea is missing.

The first version does not need to be perfect.

Feedback can make an idea stronger.

Collaboration brings skills and perspectives you may lack.

Simple ideas can require complex execution.

Adaptability is part of turning an idea into reality.

An idea can arrive in a few seconds. It might come while solving a problem at work, talking with a friend, using a product or simply wondering whether something could be done differently. Most people have ideas from time to time, but very few ever turn them into something real. The difference is rarely just about having a clever thought. An idea needs time, effort, testing and, in many cases, other people who can bring skills that the original creator does not have. That is the thinking behind a well-known observation from Jack Dorsey, the co-founder of Twitter and Square. The quote points to a simple distinction: thinking of something is only the beginning. What follows is the harder process of making it work.Dorsey’s point is not that ideas have little value. An original idea can provide the direction for a product, business or project. But an idea remains theoretical until someone starts making decisions about how it could work in practice.Execution is where those decisions begin. A person has to decide what to build first, what can be left out, what resources are needed and how the idea should change when reality does not match the original plan.The second part of the quote is just as important. Dorsey refers to attracting other people to work on the idea, recognising that large projects rarely depend on one person alone. Different people may bring technical knowledge, design skills, business experience, funding, contacts or an understanding of customers.Ideas are easy to discuss because they have no practical limitations yet. Once someone tries to build one, those limitations become visible.A product may cost more than expected. A technical problem may force a redesign. Customers may not respond as anticipated. Something that seemed essential might turn out to be unnecessary.This is why execution can change an idea rather than simply reproduce it. The original concept provides a starting point, while the process of building reveals what actually works.A founder may have the initial concept, but that does not mean they possess every skill needed to develop it.A software project might require programmers, designers, product managers and people who understand the market. A physical product could need engineers, manufacturers and distributors. Even a small personal project can become easier when someone else brings knowledge or experience that the creator lacks.Dorsey’s wording about “attracting” people also suggests that collaboration cannot simply be assumed. Others need to understand the purpose of the project and see a reason to contribute.Dorsey was born in St Louis, Missouri, in 1976 and developed an interest in computers while growing up. He became particularly interested in communication and dispatch systems, including the way information could be shared quickly between people working in different locations.That interest later became relevant to the technology projects he pursued. He studied at the Missouri University of Science and Technology before attending New York University, although he left university without completing his degree. He subsequently worked as a programmer and became involved with software relating to dispatch and real-time communication.His early career was not built around a single grand plan. Instead, several interests gradually came together around software, communication and the movement of information.Dorsey later applied his interest in communication and technology to a very different problem.In 2009, he co-founded Square with Jim McKelvey. The company developed a small card reader that could connect to a mobile device, allowing businesses and individuals to accept card payments without relying on traditional payment terminals.The device looked simple, but the system behind it was not. Payment technology involves security, financial regulations, software, hardware and relationships with financial institutions.Square eventually expanded beyond its original product into a broader range of financial services. The company changed its corporate name to Block in 2021.The contrast between Twitter and Square is useful when considering Dorsey’s quote. The initial concepts for both companies could be explained relatively simply. Building businesses around those concepts required considerably more work and the involvement of many other people.Execution is often treated as simply completing a plan. In practice, it can mean discovering that the original plan needs to change.A prototype may reveal a technical problem. Early customers may ask for something unexpected. A product that looks useful may prove difficult to operate at scale. These experiences provide information that cannot always be gained through planning alone. That is why the first version of a product does not have to be perfect. It can serve as a way of finding out what works, what does not and what needs to be changed before more resources are committed.Bringing other people into a project introduces different perspectives.A programmer might identify a technical limitation that the founder had overlooked. A designer might notice that the product is difficult to understand. Someone working with customers might discover that the problem being solved is slightly different from what the team originally assumed.These disagreements can be useful when they are handled constructively. The final product may therefore contain ideas that were not present in the original concept. That does not necessarily mean the initial idea failed. It can mean the idea developed as more information became available.There is a natural temptation to focus on the moment an idea is conceived. It feels like the creative part, and it can be exciting to imagine what something might become. The less visible work comes afterwards. Someone has to build the first version, find out whether people want it, correct mistakes and keep improving it. If the project grows, more people become involved and the work becomes divided across different areas.At that stage, the original idea is still important, but it is no longer the whole project.The principle does not apply only to technology companies or entrepreneurs. Someone may have an idea for improving a process at work, starting a community project, creating a small business or learning a new skill. The same question eventually appears: what is the first practical step?It may be as simple as making a prototype, speaking to potential users, writing down the requirements or finding someone with the missing expertise. Starting small can also make an idea easier to evaluate. Instead of trying to prove that the entire concept will work, a person can test one part of it.Ideas have become easier to share, but turning them into functioning products, businesses or projects still takes practical work.Dorsey’s experience reflects that gap. Twitter began with a relatively simple communication concept, while Square started with a straightforward approach to accepting card payments. Both eventually required large teams and complex systems.His quote captures the distinction in simple terms. Having an idea is common. Making it work requires execution, and building something substantial often requires other people willing to take part in the process.
Article Summary: Jack Dorsey is the co-founder of Twitter and Square. He said: ‘It’s really about executing the idea and attracting other people to help you work on the idea’ An idea needs time, effort, testing and other people who can bring skills that the original creator does not have.

Article Title: Marvel's Spider-Man: Brand New Day faces AI controversy
Article Text:
Marvel's $2 billion Spider-Man hit is facing AI backlash over one artbook image

Two taxis warping into each other and a fire escape twisting into stairs that go nowhere: the telltale signs fans spotted in "Big City, Little Spider"

Marvel's AI problem did not start with this artbook

Spider-Man: Brand New Day has crossed $2 billion worldwide. It opened to $360 million in North America, the biggest domestic opening weekend in history, and roughly $932 million globally, second only to Avengers: Endgame. By every commercial measure, this is the most successful thing Marvel Studios has done in years. And now it has an AI problem, sitting inside a $50 hardcover that fans have already bought."The Art of Spider-Man: Brand New Day" reached shelves on August 18, a 208-page collector's book, and readers working through it have flagged one piece of concept art that looks machine-generated. The image is titled "Big City, Little Spider" and credited to concept artist Scott McInnes. At a glance it is an ordinary New York street, all yellow cabs and walk-up buildings. Zoom in and it falls apart. Two taxis heading in opposite directions fuse into each other mid-frame. A fire escape on the left twists into stairs that go nowhere. Traffic lights sit at strange angles. Windows land where no working artist would put them.The find surfaced through The Artbook Collector, was reported by The Direct, and spread across X, Reddit and ResetEra within hours.The complaint is specific rather than abstract. A film clearing $2 billion apparently could not pay a human to draw a taxi correctly. Readers who went through the rest of the book say the other pages look clean, which suggests one image slipped past quality control rather than a pattern running through the collection.McInnes has a serious blockbuster résumé, including Morbius, The Fantastic Four: First Steps, Guardians of the Galaxy, Andor, Barbie and Wonka. That history is part of why the reaction has been so sharp.The timing helps nobody. Marvel cut a large chunk of its visual development team months ago, the people who build a film's look before cameras roll. Fans drew their own conclusions then. Secret Invasion's AI-assisted title sequence from 2023 still gets brought up. DC recently pulled a Supergirl behind-the-scenes video after viewers spotted AI concept art of Jason Momoa's Lobo.Marvel has not commented. Buyers found out after paying.
Article Summary: Marvel's $2 billion Spider-Man hit is facing AI backlash over one artbook image. The image is titled "Big City, Little Spider" and credited to concept artist Scott McInnes. Two taxis warping into each other and a fire escape twisting into stairs that go nowhere.

Article Title: In 2023, Canadian wildfires cut solar power generation by 6.38 TWh across North America and Europe, causing an estimated $1.9 billion loss
Article Text:
Representative Image

How Canadian wildfire smoke affected solar power generation

Other factors affecting solar power generation

Wildfires can also damage solar panels and equipment

Wildfires may be adversely affecting solar power generation worldwide. According to a recent study published in Nature, smoke from the Canadian wildfires in 2023 reduced solar electricity generation across North America and Europe by an estimated 6.38 terawatt-hours (TWh) over five months. The researchers estimated that the reduction amounted to about 2.8% of the solar electricity generated across the two regions during that period.The report also estimated that the decline in solar generation caused an economic loss of about $1.9 billion and was associated with about 2.1 megatons of CO2 emissions. Researchers attributed the drop to smoke and airborne particles from the wildfires that blocked or scattered sunlight before it could reach solar panels, though they noted significant uncertainty around the estimates.The 2023 Canadian wildfire season produced large amounts of smoke that travelled across North America and reached parts of Europe. The researchers modelled the atmospheric effects of the wildfire emissions over five months to estimate their impact on solar electricity generation.Sunlight is absorbed and scattered by particles in the atmosphere. This results in less sunlight reaching the solar panels, and installations producing less electricity even if the panels themselves are not directly affected by fire.The findings also show how the effects of wildfires can extend beyond areas immediately surrounding the fires. Solar farms, commercial installations and rooftop systems can all be affected when smoke moves through the atmosphere above them.Wildfire smoke is not the only source of air pollution that decreases the productivity of solar panel arrays. Pollution particles (particulate matter) released into the air by automobiles and coal-burning electrical generators may decrease how much sunlight enters your solar array.Dust can affect panels in different ways by settling directly on the panel surface . Dust accumulation from construction and mining activities can reduce electricity generation if panels are not cleaned.Improved solar-power forecasting can help grid operators prepare for generation changes caused by smoke. More accurate forecasts can help operators anticipate declines in solar output and arrange alternative electricity sources to maintain the balance between supply and demand.According to Cornell University, researchers studied a machine learning model for predicting solar energy production during certain extreme wildfire smoke OPS events in 2025. Researchers indicated that the model has more detail and accuracy than the New York grid operator's forecasts.Emissions from automobiles and factories are a source of atmospheric pollution. These can be reduced with improved dust management at solar farms. This will limit the effects of pollution on the farms’ ability to generate electricity.Wildfire smoke can affect solar generation without physically damaging an installation, but fires can also directly threaten solar farms. The U.S. Department of Energy has identified wildfire damage as a risk to photovoltaic systems, including potential damage to panels and components used to operate them.A solar farm owned by a French company Luxel was affected by a wildfire last month. The fire broke out in southern France in July 2026. About 100 of the 43,500 panels and some cables were damaged in the blaze, while the transformers and inverters were not harmed.Vegetation management around the site helped limit the fire's reach. Luxel said that regular clearing work, including a 50-meter perimeter around the fences, helped prevent flames from reaching most of the installation.The US Department of Energy recommends maintaining defensible space around solar installations in areas exposed to wildfire risk. Its measures include managing vegetation, paving areas around critical equipment, placing important electrical components in fire-resistant containers, maintaining access for firefighters and keeping an updated wildfire emergency-response plan.The Canadian wildfire study illustrates how fires can affect solar power production without reaching a solar energy facility, and physical damage to infrastructure is an additional risk to facilities built in wildland-urban interface areas.
Article Summary: Smoke from the Canadian wildfires in 2023 reduced solar electricity generation across North America and Europe by an estimated 6.38 terawatt-hours. The decline in solar generation caused an economic loss of about $1.9 billion and was associated with about 2.1 megatons of CO2 emissions. Researchers attributed the drop to smoke and airborne particles from the wildfires.

Article Title: Startup founded by three Harvard dropouts that tech investors warned of saying 'don’t back kids in chips' is pulling talent from Nvidia; engineer says ...
Article Text:
Etched co-founders Robert Wachen, Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu. (Image source: WSJ)

Investors once warned ‘Don’t back the kids in chips’

Etched is hiring from Nvidia

A chip startup once viewed by investors as too inexperienced to take on the semiconductor industry is now pulling engineers from Nvidia and other major chip companies, as it moves closer to becoming a serious player in AI hardware. Etched, founded by three 24-year-old Harvard dropouts, has signed quantitative-trading firm Jane Street as its first customer, booked more than $1 billion in orders and started shipping its AI chips. The hiring trend has also surprised some of its new employees. Former Nvidia systems engineer Anthony Gamerman said he kept hearing about colleagues leaving Nvidia for Etched. “One leaves, and then another one, you hear a couple weeks later, and you go, ‘Whoa, I can’t believe so-and-so is heading over to Etched,’” he said.Etched was started by Robert Wachen, Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu, who are all 24 years old. The company initially struggled to attract investors because of the founders' limited experience in semiconductor hardware.Sonya Huang, a general partner at Sequoia Capital, described the concern among investors at the time. “Among tech investors, the prevailing wisdom was ‘don’t back the kids in chips,’” Huang said.She added that investors believed young founders could succeed in internet businesses but faced much bigger challenges when building semiconductor hardware.Etched has since raised nearly $2 billion, including a new $700 million funding round led by Jane Street that values the company at $21 billion.The startup has built a team with significant semiconductor experience. Around 15% of its roughly 400 employees previously worked at Nvidia, according to Etched. The company has also hired engineers from other established semiconductor firms.Brian Loiler, who spent nearly 23 years at Nvidia, joined Etched to work on its servers and racks. He has since helped recruit about a dozen Nvidia engineers to the startup, with some turning down counteroffers. Jimmy Daley, a former Nvidia vice president of data-center systems engineering who retired in July, is also an investor in Etched.The company has developed AI processors designed specifically for this workload. Its first customer is Jane Street, a quantitative trading firm that uses powerful computing systems to run trading models quickly. Etched says it has already started shipping its chips and took just 44 days to get its test chips running inference workloads after receiving them from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.“We may be the only AI chip that was built by a startup that was successful on the first try,” Etched co-founder and president Robert Wachen said.
Article Summary: Etched, founded by three 24-year-old Harvard dropouts, has signed quantitative- trading firm Jane Street as its first customer. The company has booked more than $1 billion in orders and started shipping its AI chips. Around 15% of its roughly 400 employees previously worked at Nvidia.

Article Title: Anthropic is about to sell you the company it keeps warning you about
Article Text:
Anthropic accounts for around 60% of the combined revenue estimate of Starbucks and McDonald's

The warnings that built the company become paperwork the moment they are filed

The men warning about concentrated power are about to concentrate some

The forecast and the warning describe the same two years

The contradiction does not get resolved, only priced

Every company that goes public has to write down all the ways it might destroy itself.It is called the risk factors section. It runs for dozens of pages, it is written by lawyers, and almost nobody reads it. Bankers tolerate it. Investors skip past it to the growth charts. It exists so that when something goes badly wrong three years later, the company can point at page 47 and say the warning was always there, in the document you signed off on.Anthropic has been reading its risk factors section out loud for five years.That is the peculiar thing about what is coming. Anthropic expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX's record IPO, according to Bloomberg, and could file publicly as soon as the end of this month. SpaceX raised $75 billion at the outset, rising to $86.2 billion once the overallotment was exercised, the biggest first-time share sale ever recorded.Anthropic is running the numbers on doing that or better, with Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase on the deal. The Wall Street Journal puts the debut at September or early October. The last private round, in May, valued the company at $965 billion. It was founded in 2021.None of that is the contradiction. Enormous IPOs happen. Fast growth happens, though rarely at this speed. The contradiction is that Anthropic's whole reason for existing as a separate company from the one its founders walked out of rests on the argument that this technology is dangerous enough to require restraint. And restraint is the one thing a public market does not know how to price.It helps to be precise about what Anthropic sells, because it is not only software. Dario Amodei left OpenAI in 2021 and built a company around a claim: that frontier AI is powerful enough to be hazardous, that the people building it should say so plainly, and that a lab willing to slow itself down is a lab worth trusting with the hard stuff.He has said versions of this on podcasts, in essays, in front of lawmakers, at his own company's Builder Summit in Bengaluru in February. Last week Anthropic published a substantive risk report, per The Information, laying out what its researchers are finding about models that scheme and work against the goals assigned to them. That is not a document most companies publish weeks before the largest IPO in history.And it worked. Not despite the warnings. Because of them. The safety framing is what made Anthropic the vendor cautious enterprises and regulated industries could sign with, and the numbers are the proof.CNBC has confirmed the annualised revenue run rate hit $65 billion at the end of July, a sevenfold jump in a year, up from roughly $9 billion at the end of 2025. Second-quarter revenue crossed $11.5 billion against $787 million a year earlier. OpenAI, over the same three months, booked $6.7 billion.Then the prospectus lands, and every one of those warnings changes function.They stop being conviction and become legal artefacts, restated in the flat defensive register of securities law. Risks related to our models. Risks related to our regulatory environment. Once a warning sits in that section it is no longer a signal of seriousness, it is a shield against being sued for the thing you warned about.The audience changes with it. For five years Amodei was talking to governments, researchers and the public. From the day of the filing he is talking to shareholders, a constituency with exactly one question, asked quarterly.The financials make that question sharp. Anthropic posted a net loss of almost $42 billion in 2025, roughly five times the year before, on revenue of about $10 billion, according to documents seen by Bloomberg. Reuters has the second quarter delivering a first operating profit of $559 million, which is a real turn.But the spending behind those losses has not slowed. One compute agreement with SpaceX alone could be worth tens of billions of dollars over three years. A company burning at that scale has very little room to make an expensive decision on principle, and even less once the burn is public.Anthropic knows all of this. You can tell, because of what it is building to defend itself.The company has been preparing a class of stock with extra voting power for Amodei and his six co-founders, The Information first revealed, which would be the first time Anthropic's leaders held voting rights beyond their ownership. The mechanism is ordinary in Silicon Valley. Meta, Snap and SpaceX all did it.What makes it unusual here is the arithmetic. Amodei owns about 2 percent of the company he founded, a person close to it told the same publication, his stake diluted by hundreds of billions in outside capital. That may be the smallest founder holding of any chief executive taking a company public in decades.Sitting alongside it is the Long-Term Benefit Trust, created in 2023, holding Class T shares with no economic value and one real power: electing the majority of Anthropic's seven-person board. Ben Bernanke is a trustee. The trust is currently down to three members from its usual five, after Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar left this month to become Anthropic's chief global affairs officer.Read that structure plainly and it is an admission. Anthropic is inviting the public markets in and bolting the doors from the inside on the way. Supervoting shares insulate the founders from shareholder pressure. The trust keeps the board.The company also stays a public benefit corporation, legally permitted to weigh society against returns, which will make it by an enormous margin the largest such entity on any US exchange. The next biggest is Veeva Systems, at $40 billion.Amodei's defence writes itself, and it is not a bad one: the point of the shares is to protect the mission from precisely the short-term pressure the listing invites. But a man who has spent years warning that AI risks concentrating power in too few hands is about to be handed more of it.You also cannot argue that outside shareholders will push a company toward decisions it should not make and simultaneously argue that selling them the company is fine. Both cannot be true. The governance structure is Anthropic conceding the first one.The valuation math tells you what investors are actually buying, and it is not caution. Anthropic is projecting 2028 revenue of roughly $190 billion to $200 billion, Reuters has learnt, with bankers valuing the company off that number two years out. The comparison set includes Palantir, which trades at 53 times this year's expected revenue, and Cloudflare and SpaceX, both around 41 times.Apply anything like those multiples and a $2 trillion debut stops being a fantasy. That is roughly where one investor landed when the news agency asked him, his question being not whether Anthropic could get there but whether it would stay.Hold that forecast against the safety argument. To go from $65 billion annualised to $200 billion booked inside two and a half years, Claude has to be inside almost everything, including healthcare and biology, which is where the company has told investors it plans to push next.That is not a scenario with a pause in it. That is maximum deployment at maximum speed, in exactly the window Amodei has described as the one where models get capable enough to be dangerous.He has already shown what a pause costs. In June, Anthropic temporarily disabled access to Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 to comply with a US export control directive citing national security authorities, and got them back roughly two weeks later after tense negotiation and some concessions.Earlier this year the Pentagon blacklisted the company after talks over military use collapsed on the limits Anthropic wanted, and the two sides are still in court. Investors have been pressing executives on exactly this in pre-IPO meetings, the Journal found, alongside cheap Chinese models and the backlash to data centre construction.Anthropic absorbed all of it as a private company, because the only people owed an explanation were investors already committed and reachable in a room. Do the same fortnight as a listed company and it is a material event, a stock move, a set of analyst notes, and a class of shareholders asking why management picked a fight it could have avoided.The willingness to lose money over a limit is what made the safety position credible. After the listing, that willingness has a price, it is visible to everyone, and somebody will eventually argue in court that paying it was a breach of duty.Both things stay true, and one of them starts trading. The safety mission is not being abandoned, and the people running Anthropic are not cynics who stopped believing their own case. But an IPO does one thing above all others. It converts a private conviction into a number that trades, and hands the number to strangers.Anthropic has spent five years telling the world this technology is too important to be governed by people chasing quarterly returns. In September or October it will sell that world a large stake in itself and invite exactly those people to the table.The supervoting shares, the trust, the benefit corporation charter are all attempts to take the capital without the consequence. They will hold, or they will not. Nobody knows yet, because the first real test has not arrived.But it will. There will come a quarter when the safe decision and the profitable one point in opposite directions, and unlike every previous instance, the whole market will be watching which way Anthropic goes. Every buyer will have been warned before that quarter arrives, by the people who stand to make the most from being wrong.Anthropic said it out loud for five years. From the filing onwards, it says it on page 47.
Article Summary: Anthropic has been reading its risk factors section out loud for five years. The company has been preparing a class of stock with extra voting power. It could file publicly as soon as the end of this month. Anthropic expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX's record IPO.

Article Title: ChatGPT prompts used by expert witness to write report defending 3M in explosion at Watson Grinding presented in court, here's the 'important lesson' it gives
Article Text:
Representative image

"create an exceptional expert witness report defending the standard of care at 3M"

"show how 3M is 0% at fault for the explosion at Watson Grinding."

"90 to 85% ChatGPT."

ChatGPT prompts used for the 3M expert report

"Citation Overlay"

"From a technical and standard-of-care standpoint, 3M is 0% responsible for the January 24, 2020 explosion."

Expert witness used ChatGPT to revise and assess report

"What am I looking at?"

"I've got a body of work and 20-plus years of experience in the industry,"

"My opinions were put in there, and AI helped me to draft a straw man to build off of."

"I put information and opinions in up front before it ever generated […] if the output wasn't of my opinion or what I agreed to, I did alter it."

"sitting in traffic"

"jog my memory"

ChatGPT conversations became part of court discovery

"This expert relied on AI not as an assistive device, but exclusively relied on ChatGPT to form his opinions and write his report,"

"He acknowledged [at trial] the prompts he put in were biased toward 3M to help 3M win the case […] it’s really egregious."

3M hired an expert witness to prepare a report about a 2020 Houston explosion that killed three people and destroyed roughly 200 homes. The witness reportedly used ChatGPT to write significant portions of his expert report, with the use of AI coming to light after prompts he used while preparing the report were revealed during court proceedings.The prompts showed that Josh Autenrieth of Knighthawk Engineering asked ChatGPT to help himand toDuring testimony, Autenrieth acknowledged using ChatGPT and said the submitted report wasThe case concerns the January 2020 explosion at Watson Grinding, a Houston manufacturing facility. The US Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board said a degraded, poorly crimped rubber welding hose caused the explosion by leaking flammable gas.Dozens of homeowners sued 3M and Watson Grinding over the explosion. Plaintiffs alleged that 3M failed to properly service the facility's gas detection system and made other errors that contributed to the incident.As part of the litigation, 3M hired Autenrieth to prepare an expert report addressing the company's role in the explosion. During discovery, plaintiffs' attorney Will Moye found a five-page document calledthat appeared to have been generated using AI.Moye asked 3M's lawyers for the prompts Autenrieth had used. The deposition was paused for three hours while the material was collected, and Moye received about 350 pages of ChatGPT conversations.Autenrieth had told ChatGPT that he was being retained by 3M to defend the company and needed to prepare an expert report concerning its standard of care. He uploaded hundreds of court records and instructed the chatbot to review them and support 3M's position.ChatGPT initially generated a roughly 30-page report containing the statement,That wording was later removed after Autenrieth asked ChatGPT to assess the report from the perspective of opposing counsel.The ChatGPT conversations showed that Autenrieth repeatedly uploaded versions of the report and asked the chatbot to revise them. He also asked it to grade the report and identify arguments the opposing side could challenge.At one point, ChatGPT gave the report a score of 97 out of 100. Autenrieth also asked it to identify the five main issues in the report that the opposing side could attack and how he could respond.In another conversation, he uploaded an image of a gas detector and asked ChatGPT,He also asked about model names of industrial gas detectors. The gas detection system was central to the plaintiffs' allegations against 3M.Autenrieth also asked ChatGPT whether his resume was sufficient for him to serve as an expert witness and whether his lack of previous experience as an expert witness could be raised during the case.The report eventually submitted to the court followed the structure of ChatGPT's initial output, while substantial portions were identical to the chatbot's original response and subsequent revisions.Autenrieth acknowledged using ChatGPT but maintained that his professional experience remained the basis for his opinions.Autenrieth said.He described the AI's role by saying,He also said,Autenrieth said he also used ChatGPT whiletoabout different manufacturers of gas detectors.The disclosure of the prompts also highlighted how AI conversations used while preparing litigation materials can become relevant during discovery or depositions. Moye said the case showed why lawyers need to consider how their expert witnesses use AI when preparing reports.Moye told 404 Media.Moye said 3M later tried to have Autenrieth disqualified from the trial. After learning about the extent of his AI use, Moye instead called the opposing expert as a witness so the jury could hear about the report.The jury ultimately awarded more than $61 million to the plaintiffs and assigned 30% of the responsibility to 3M and 70% to Watson Grinding. Earlier decisions had also awarded $118 million and $38 million to victims of the explosion.The case is among several instances in which AI-generated material has emerged in legal proceedings. In France, AI was used to make an argument about rainwater patterns in a flooding dispute, while in Canada, a judge gave no weight to an AI-generated opinion concerning plants and a bug infestation.The Watson Grinding case shows that prompts and AI conversations can form part of the record when an expert's use of an AI system becomes relevant to litigation. For lawyers and expert witnesses, the case also demonstrates that using an AI chatbot while preparing court testimony does not necessarily keep the underlying prompts outside the discovery process.
Article Summary: ChatGPT conversations became part of court discovery. Josh Autenrieth of Knighthawk Engineering asked ChatGPT to help him and to write his report. He also asked the chatbot to grade the report and identify arguments the opposing side could challenge. The case concerns the January 2020 explosion at Watson Grinding.

Article Title: Government orders Google to shut down hundreds of Firebase accounts after finding pattern of the service being misused by criminals
Article Text:
Representative Image

"strict policies prohibiting the use of our services for phishing, malware, or

financial fraud

"

Google Firebase accounts targeted in India

Android malware used in banking scams

"Android-based malware programs are masquerading as legitimate banking services, specifically targeting Android users with credit cards. Scammers lure victims by promoting offers such as new credit cards, reward redemptions, or credit limit upgrades,"

India steps up action against online scams

"Android God Mode".

"These malicious apps often impersonate trusted services such as banking, government and utility platforms, and trick users into installing them through links,"

The government has directed Google to shut down hundreds of accounts on its Firebase web development platform. A report by the news agency Reuters cited government notices and a source familiar with the matter, saying the order came after officials found a pattern of criminals using the service to impersonate major banks and defraud people. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) directed Google to remove at least 57 websites and databases hosted on Firebase in August alone, saying they were being used to distribute malware and steal sensitive financial information.The notices, reviewed by the news agency, said the websites were being used in scams targeting Android users, including schemes that mimicked banking services and collected financial information from victims' phones. Google said it hasand works with law enforcement, including I4C, to evaluate and act on notices.The I4C issued at least three notices to Google in August directing the removal of the 57 websites and databases. The notices said the links were involved in malware distribution and the theft of sensitive information. Google can be held liable for the named links if they are not removed within three hours of a notice being issued.The notices did not suggest that Google or Firebase was responsible for the scams. The source, who has direct knowledge of the matter, said Indian officials had identified a pattern in recent months involving scammers using Firebase, Google's app and website development platform.The source said the number of notices sent to Google over Firebase had reached dozens in recent months, although an exact figure was not provided.Seven of the websites and databases identified in the August notices were phishing pages created using Firebase that mimicked Indian banks, including State Bank of India, ICICI Bank and Axis Bank. The government agency described the remaining websites as being used to collect data stolen from victims' phones, including credit card details and one-time passwords.In an August 17 notice, I4C said scammers were using Android-based malware programs that masqueraded as legitimate banking services and targeted Android users with credit cards.I4C said in the notice seen by Reuters.The scams involved convincing victims to install applications that appeared to be legitimate banking services. Once installed, the applications could send information from the user's phone to a Firebase database controlled by the scammers.One scheme identified by officials involved PM-KISAN, a federal government programme that provides payments to small farmers. According to a government notice and the source, scam websites promised recipients assistance in claiming their payments and asked them to download an application to redeem the money.The application then sent user data to the scammers' Firebase database, allowing them to access information from other applications on the phone and potentially use it to defraud victims.The action against Firebase-based scams comes as Indian authorities increase efforts to tackle online financial fraud. Government data shows that Indians lost nearly $2.4 billion in alleged cyber fraud in 2025.Indian officials have traditionally targeted scam websites by ordering their removal. The notices reviewed by Reuters indicate that authorities are also examining the infrastructure used to distribute malicious applications and collect information from victims.The government issued a public advisory in March warning about a form of malware that cybersecurity researchers widely refer to asThe term describes malicious software that can give scammers extensive control over victims' Android phones.the advisory said.Google said it works with law enforcement agencies, including I4C, when evaluating notices involving potential policy violations.
Article Summary: Indian government orders Google to shut down hundreds of Firebase accounts. Officials found a pattern of criminals using the service to impersonate major banks and defraud people. Google said it works with law enforcement agencies, including I4C, to evaluate and act on notices.

Article Title: In 2020, Nvidia launched AI chip that is still going strong; Cloud computing company signs contract to rent them till 2029
Article Text:
‘Proving the AI chip doubters wrong’

Artificial intelligence (AI) cloud provider CoreWeave recently confirmed a long-term agreement to lease out Nvidia A100 graphics processing units into 2029, essentially providing a real-world solution of the ongoing problem (and debate) over how long AI processors remain commercially viable. Speaking with financial analysts, CoreWeave CFO Nitin Agrawal revealed the multi-year deal for the processors, which Nvidia originally launched in 2020. The contract guarantees that enterprise clients will continue utilising the hardware for active computing workloads nearly a full decade after its initial market debut. This comes as companies struggle to secure advanced AI chips amid a rapidly growing market.The longevity of computing silicon sits at the centre of concerns surrounding the AI boom. According to a report by Business Insider, market critics and short sellers have frequently asserted that fast product cycles from hardware manufacturers would render older processors obsolete in two to three years. This rapid turnover would force cloud providers to write down multibillion-dollar data center investments quickly, cutting into corporate earnings.However, CoreWeave’s operational numbers point to sustained commercial demand. Agrawal confirmed that the extended A100 deal was closed at strong financial terms, adding that CoreWeave has largely exhausted its rental inventory across earlier-generation Nvidia processors.Citing industry pricing tracker Silicon Data, the report said that rental pricing for A100 processors has stabilised following a sharp recovery in 2026 and the practical economic lifespan of high-end GPUs clearly extends beyond the two-to-three-year timeline assumed by skeptics.Industry operators explain that aging graphics hardware continues to deliver steady revenue because computing needs diversify after initial system development. It is to be noted that cutting-edge processors remain necessary to train leading foundation models everyday computing workload can run effectively on earlier silicon.Hardware longevity takes on added urgency as global asset managers commit huge capital toward data centres. Nvidia unveiled strategic alliances with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR designed to direct more than $500 billion into infrastructure over time.
Article Summary: Cloud provider CoreWeave confirmed a long-term agreement to lease out Nvidia A100 graphics processing units into 2029. The contract guarantees that enterprise clients will continue utilising the hardware for active computing workloads. This comes as companies struggle to secure advanced AI chips amid a growing market.

Article Title: Quote of the day by John D. Rockefeller: If your only goal is to become rich, you will never achieve it
Article Text:
Quote of the day by John D. Rockefeller: If your only goal is to become rich, you will never achieve it

What John D. Rockefeller’s quote means

Other famous quotes by John D. Rockefeller

“I would rather earn 1% off a 100 people's efforts than 100% of my own efforts.”

“Go as far as you can see; when you get there, you'll be able to see farther.”

“Success comes from keeping the ears open and the mouth closed" ~ John D. Rockefeller”

“It is one thing to stand on the comfortable ground of placid inaction and put forth words of cynical wisdom, and another to plunge into the work itself and through strenuous experience earn the right to express strong conclusions.”

“Nobody does anything if he can get anybody else to do it”

John D. Rockefeller was one of the richest businessmen in American history. He is fondly remembered for his approach to money, business and success. One quote often linked to him is: “If your only goal is to become rich, you will never achieve it. ” The quote highlights the idea that wealth should not be the only goal behind a person's work. Instead, success can come from building something valuable, working consistently and focusing on long-term goals.John D. Rockefeller was an American businessman and philanthropist. He built his fortune through the oil industry and became one of the most powerful businessmen of his time. He co-founded Standard Oil in 1870. The company grew rapidly and became a major force in the US oil industry.Rockefeller later became known for giving away a large part of his wealth. His donations supported education, medical research and other causes.John D. Rockefeller’s quote suggests that chasing money alone may not be the best way to build wealth. People who focus only on becoming rich may overlook the work needed to create a successful business or career.Building useful products, solving problems and developing skills can create value that eventually leads to financial success.The message also points to the importance of having a larger purpose. Money can be an important goal. But focusing on skills, work and long-term growth can provide a stronger path toward success.Rockefeller's own life is often used to illustrate this approach. His wealth came from building a large business over many years, while his later philanthropy helped shape his legacy beyond his fortune.
Article Summary: John D. Rockefeller was an American businessman and philanthropist. He built his fortune through the oil industry and became one of the most powerful businessmen of his time. One quote often linked to him is: “If your only goal is to become rich, you will never achieve it ”

Article Title: Sony India launches FE 100-400mm F5.6-8 OSS at Rs 94,990
Article Text:
Sony's new 400mm lens weighs less than most 70-200s

Sony India has launched the FE 100-400mm F5.6-8 OSS, a full-frame super telephoto zoom that weighs 654 grams and sells for Rs 94,990. It is available from August 20 across Sony Centers, Alpha Flagship stores, authorised dealers and major electronics chains, plus Amazon and Flipkart.The weight is the headline. At 654g and 165.5mm long, this is a 400mm lens you can hang off a shoulder strap through a full morning at a sanctuary without your neck filing a complaint. Add a teleconverter and the reach stretches to 800mm, which is the kind of number that usually comes attached to a tripod and a porter.The optics do the usual heavy lifting: two ED glass elements and two aspherical elements to hold sharpness from centre to edge, and a 9-blade circular aperture for rounder, softer backgrounds. More interesting is the close-focus figure. The FE 100-400mm F5.6-8 OSS focuses down to 0.86m with 0.41x maximum magnification, which is unusually tight for a lens of this reach and effectively hands you a pseudo-macro at the long end.Autofocus runs on dual linear motors, quiet and quick enough for birds in flight and athletes mid-sprint. Optical SteadyShot handles the handheld shake that becomes unforgiving past 300mm. On the barrel, Sony has fitted a focus hold button, a focus-mode and range switch, and a zoom lock, with dust and moisture resistance for the days the weather turns.There is a sustainability angle too. Over 41 percent of the lens's total plastic weight is recycled, rising to more than 89 percent in the hood and 88 percent in the caps.The tradeoff sits in the name. F8 at 400mm asks for good light, and shooters who chase the last twenty minutes of golden hour will feel it. Everyone else gets a super telephoto that finally fits in the bag.
Article Summary: The FE 100-400mm F5.6-8 OSS is a full-frame super telephoto zoom that weighs 654 grams and sells for Rs 94,990. It is available from August 20 across Sony Centers, Alpha Flagship stores, authorised dealers and major electronics chains, plus Amazon and Flipkart.
